subject: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?

messages.author: c11f259197c4042d
messages.subject: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?
parts:
Hello everyone
I'm working with a camera trap dataset to study the habitat characteristics that determine carnivore presence.  We have 10 years of data, but and at this point we are not interested in yearly dynamics (mostly because likely we do not have enough data). The sampling effort is quite unbalanced (different amounts of effort in different years, both the number of cameras and time active). 
Because of sparse detections we think that stacking years might be the best option. I've seen in different messages in the forum that for similar cases is recommended to use single-season occupancy models on the stacked data but also an N-mixture model was recommended. Both cases using non-parametric bootstrapping. 

For my case, would you recommend single-season occupancy or N-mixture? If is the second case would you point me to some place to find more information on model implementation? 

Thanks a lot for your help!

Cheers

Juan

messages.author: 97512b0c9bacfbef
messages.subject: Re: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?
parts:
Hi Natalia,

I'm far less knowledgeable than many on this forum, but I think you're right that if data from each year were from different sites, you would not be able to separate the differences in year from the differences in site.  So, you might still be able to stack the data and get an estimate of overall occupancy, but with confounded variables (site and year) you wouldn't know what is causing any differences.  If you did stack them, you would need to include a covariate to represent the site/year, knowing this variable is confounded but perhaps helpful in getting overall estimates.  I think, particularly with scarce data, you would have to have some repeated measures in your data (within each site/year) in order for the models to run.  Either way, you'd need to be sure not to violate the assumption of closure.

To Juan's original post, N-mixture models estimate abundance.  To estimate presence, you need to use an occupancy model.  Further, in my experience N-mix models need more data to converge than occupancy models, so with sparse detections, occupancy models are probably a safer bet.

-Alex

messages.author: 198c44d635827adf
messages.subject: Re: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?
parts:
Juan and Natalia,

You can stack your data since you are not worried about yearly turnover rates. It does not matter that you surveyed different sites in different years when you are strictly investigating habitat variables associated with occupancy. This topic is covered in the McKenzie et al. book (Occupancy Estimation and Modeling Inferring Patterns and Dynamics of Species Occurrence). 

Juan,

Since you are using camera trap data I highly recommend the Royle and Nichols 2003 model (Royle, J. A., & Nichols, J. D. (2003). Estimating abundance from repeated presence–absence data or point counts. Ecology, 84(3), 777-790.) since the model accounts for unmodeled heterogeneity in detection among sites. Which is extremely common in camera trap data. The model does produce an abundance estimate; however, you can convert it to psi. The function in unmark to convert the estimate is lambda2psi.      

As for model implementation I would recommend choosing the number of surveys that you feel is appropriate (possibly the max number of surveys conducted over the 10 years) and fill in NAs for any missing data like you would for nonstacked data. Each site would then have its own covariates that are associated with it in the SiteCovs of the unmarked frame.  Since the surveys were taken at different times over a long survey period I would recommend modeling a Julian date  covariate in your detection model.

-Ryan
